# Lynch syndrome

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Lynch syndrome*

[Original Article Link](/library/fS0k_2)

---

## Summary

Lynch syndrome, or hereditary nonpolyposis <u>colon cancer</u> (HNPCC), is a <u>familial cancer syndrome</u> caused by an <u>autosomal dominant</u> mutation in <u>DNA mismatch repair</u> (MMR) <u>genes</u>. Affected individuals develop a small number of <u>adenomas</u> that can rapidly progress to <u>colorectal cancer</u> (<u>CRC</u>), resulting in a considerably earlier symptom onset compared to sporadic <u>colorectal cancer</u>. Individuals with Lynch syndrome are also at increased risk of developing other forms of cancer, especially <u>endometrial</u>, gastric, and <u>ovarian cancer</u>. Individuals are asymptomatic until they present with symptoms of <u>advanced cancer</u>. To identify those at high risk for Lynch syndrome, individuals are assessed according to the Amsterdam II criteria. Subsequent <u>genetic analysis</u> with detection of MMR mutations confirms the diagnosis. Treatment of <u>CRC</u> consists of surgical <u>colectomy</u> and immunotherapy. Preventative <u>screening for colorectal cancer</u> and associated tumors is recommended in individuals with family members known to have a Lynch syndrome <u>gene</u> mutation; it should occur every 1–2 years, starting at 20–25 years of age, or 2–5 years before the earliest recorded case of a <u>tumor</u> in the family.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u>

* Most common cause of inherited <u>CRC</u>

* Accounts for approx. 3–8% of all new cases of <u>CRC</u>

* Individuals with Lynch syndrome have a 70–80% lifetime risk of developing <u>CRC</u>

* Sex: <u>♂</u> = <u>♀</u>

* Average age of onset: 44 years

* Increased lifetime risk of associated cancers (by age 70) 

* <u>Endometrial cancer</u>: up to 40%

* <u>Gastric cancer</u>: ∼ 10%

* <u>Ovarian tumors</u>: ∼ 10%

* <u>Urothelial cancer</u>: up to 10%

* <u>Skin</u>: ∼ 4%

* <u>Small bowel cancer</u>: ∼ 2%

* <u>Brain tumor</u>: ∼ 2%

* <u>Biliary tract cancer</u>: ∼ 2%





References:[[1]](/library/0aYeQn)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Hereditary disease: <u>autosomal dominant</u> with varying <u>penetrance</u>

* Mutations in various <u>DNA mismatch repair genes</u> (<u>MLH1</u>, <u>MSH2</u>, MSH6, PMS2) cause <u>microsatellite instability</u>.
* Increased occurrence of <u>adenomas</u> with ∼ 80% risk of progression to <u>carcinomas</u>





![Colorectal carcinogenesis pathways](media/m2oz8iszukfh1lk5by22nzyv.jpg)

Colorectal carcinogenesis pathways




References:[[2]](/library/b60HjS)

---

## Clinical features

* Patients are usually asymptomatic until <u>CRC</u> develops (see <u>colorectal cancer</u>).

* Lynch syndrome-associated <u>CRC</u> usually affects the right (<u>proximal</u>) <u>colon</u>.

* Possibly extracolonic symptoms of associated cancers (see “<u>Epidemiology</u>” section above)





References:[[2]](/library/b60HjS)

---

## Subtypes and variants

* Muir-Torre syndrome

* A variant of Lynch syndrome caused by mutations also occurring in <u>MLH1</u>, <u>MSH2</u>, or MSH6

* Characterized by <u>sebaceous gland</u> tumors and <u>keratoacanthomas</u> in addition to Lynch syndrome-associated cancers

* <u>Turcot syndrome</u>: presence of Lynch syndrome-related <u>CRC</u> and <u>brain tumors</u> (especially <u>gliomas</u>)

* Lynch-like syndrome [[3]](/library/AhVRg80) 

* A hereditary <u>colorectal cancer</u> syndrome in which tumors show MMR deficiency and <u>microsatellite instability</u> similar to Lynch syndrome, but no pathogenic <u>germline</u> MMR <u>gene</u> variant is identified.

* Increased risk of <u>colorectal cancer</u> and extracolonic cancers (e.g., <u>endometrial cancer</u>, <u>urothelial cancer</u>, <u>gastric cancer</u>) compared to the general population

* Increased surveillance (e.g., early <u>colonoscopy</u>) is recommended for patients and <u>first-degree relatives</u>; intervals should be individualized based on <u>family history</u>.





References:[[4]](/library/aaYQQn)

---

## Diagnosis

Lynch syndrome should be suspected if there is a positive <u>family history</u> based on the Amsterdam II criteria. <u>Genetic testing</u> confirms the diagnosis.




### <u>Family history</u>




The Amsterdam II criteria are used to identify individuals who are likely to be mutation carriers for Lynch syndrome.




| Amsterdam II criteria |
| --- |
| <br>Presence of at least three relatives with a Lynch syndrome-associated cancer; all the following criteria should be present: <br><br>* One should be a first-degree relative of the other two<br><br>* At least two consecutive generations affected<br><br>* At least one relative with a diagnosis before 50 years of age<br><br>* Exclude cases of <u>familial adenomatous polyposis</u>.<br><br>* Verify tumors with pathological examination.<br><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> 3-2-1 rule: (3 affected family members, 2 generations, 1 relative under 50 years of age).




The <u>Revised Bethesda guidelines</u> are used to identify individuals with <u>colorectal cancer</u> who should undergo <u>tumor</u> testing for <u>microsatellite instability</u>.




| Revised Bethesda guidelines |
| --- |
| Individuals should be tested for MSI in the following situations: <br><br>* <u>Colorectal cancer</u> diagnosed in patients < 50 years<br><br>* Presence of synchronous, <u>metachronous</u> colorectal, or other Lynch syndrome-associated tumors, regardless of age<br><br>* <u>Colorectal cancer</u> with MSI-H-like <u>histology</u>  diagnosed in patients < 60 years<br><br>* <u>Colorectal cancer</u> in ≥ 1 first-degree relative(s) with a Lynch syndrome-related <u>tumor</u>, with one of the cancers being diagnosed under age 50<br><br>* <u>Colorectal cancer</u> in ≥ 2 first-degree or second-degree relatives with Lynch syndrome-related tumors, regardless of age<br><br><br><br> |





### <u>Genetic testing</u>




* First test: <u>tumor</u> <u>microsatellite instability</u> (MSI) and/or <u>immunohistochemical</u> staining (<u>IHC</u>)

* Low MSI/stable <u>microsatellite</u> and normal <u>IHC</u>: rules out Lynch syndrome

* High MSI and/or abnormal <u>IHC</u>: requires further evaluation

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>germline</u> testing via <u>DNA</u> <u>sequencing</u> 
* Detection of mutations in <u>DNA repair</u> <u>genes</u> (MLH1, <u>MSH2</u>, MSH6, and PMS2)





### <u>Colorectal cancer</u>



* For diagnosis of <u>CRC</u>, see <u>colorectal cancer</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Lynch syndrome typically manifests with <u>colorectal cancer</u> of the <u>proximal</u> <u>colon</u>, with only a few <u>adenomatous polyps</u>, in contrast to <u>familial adenomatous polyposis</u>, in which hundreds of <u>adenomatous polyps</u> are present.




References:[[2]](/library/b60HjS)[[5]](/library/31XSgC)

---

## Treatment

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Subtotal <u>colectomy</u> with ileorectal <u>anastomosis</u>

* Total <u>colectomy</u> with <u>ileostomy</u>

* Total <u>colectomy</u> with ileorectal <u>anastomosis</u>

* Immunotherapy with an <u>immune checkpoint inhibitor</u> (pembrolizumab or nivolumab) may be used for high MSI or <u>mismatch repair</u> deficient (dMMR) <u>metastatic</u> <u>colorectal cancer</u>. [[6]](/library/OsYIEq)[[7]](/library/lsYvEq)

* For more specific guidelines regarding management, see <u>colorectal cancer</u>.

* For women with Lynch syndrome, prophylactic <u>hysterectomy</u> and bilateral <u>salpingo-oophorectomy</u> should be offered when they are no longer of child-bearing age.





References:[[8]](/library/X609jS)

---

## Prevention

* <u>Genetic counseling</u>

* <u>Genetic testing</u> is generally not recommended for at-risk individuals < 18 years of age.

* Genetic screening should be initiated 10 years before the earliest manifestation of the condition in the family.

* <u>Cancer screening</u>: for Lynch syndrome patients with a confirmed mutation or who meet <u>Amsterdam criteria</u>

* <u>Colonoscopy</u>: every 1–2 years, starting at 20–25 years of age, or 2–5 years before the earliest recorded case of a <u>tumor</u> in the family (only if it occurred before 25 years of age), whichever comes first [[9]](/library/q7YC5q)

* <u>Endometrial sampling</u> every 1–2 years starting at 30–35 years of age  [[10]](/library/bodH0I0)

* Annual <u>upper endoscopy</u> with <u>biopsy</u> of the <u>gastric antrum</u> starting at 30–35 years of age

* Annual <u>physical exam</u> and <u>urinalysis</u>

* Total <u>colectomy</u>: not generally recommended in patients with normal endoscopy





References:[[2]](/library/b60HjS)[[8]](/library/X609jS)
